{{Short description|Generalisations of Serre duality in mathematics}}
In mathematics, '''coherent duality''' is any of a number of generalisations of [[Serre duality]], applying to [[coherent sheaves]], in [[algebraic geometry]] and [[complex manifold]] theory, as well as some aspects of [[commutative algebra]] that are part of the 'local' theory.

The historical roots of the theory lie in the idea of the [[adjoint linear system]] of a [[linear system of divisors]] in classical algebraic geometry. This was re-expressed, with the advent of [[sheaf theory]], in a way that made an analogy with [[Poincaré duality]] more apparent. Then according to a general principle, [[Grothendieck's relative point of view]], the theory of [[Jean-Pierre Serre]] was extended to a [[proper morphism]]; Serre duality was recovered as the case of the morphism of a [[Algebraic curve#Singularities|non-singular]] [[projective variety]] (or [[complete variety]]) to a point. The resulting theory is now sometimes called '''Serre–Grothendieck–Verdier duality''', and is a basic tool in algebraic geometry. A treatment of this theory, ''Residues and Duality'' (1966) by [[Robin Hartshorne]], became a  reference. One concrete spin-off was the [[Grothendieck residue]].

To go beyond proper morphisms, as for the versions of Poincaré duality that are not for [[closed manifold]]s, requires some version of the ''[[compact support]]'' concept. This was addressed in [[SGA2]] in terms of [[local cohomology]], and [[Grothendieck local duality]]; and subsequently. The [[Greenlees–May duality]], first formulated in 1976 by [[Ralf Strebel]] and in 1978 by [[Eben Matlis]], is part of the continuing consideration of this area.

==Adjoint functor point of view==
{{Images of sheaves}}

While Serre duality uses a [[line bundle]] or [[invertible sheaf]] as a '''[[dualizing sheaf]]''', the general theory (it turns out) cannot be quite so simple. (More precisely, it can, but at the cost of imposing the [[Gorenstein ring]] condition.) In a characteristic turn, Grothendieck reformulated general coherent duality as the existence of a [[right adjoint]] functor <math>f^{!}</math>, called ''twisted'' or ''[[exceptional inverse image functor]]'', to a higher [[direct image with compact support]] functor <math>Rf_{!}</math>.

''Higher direct images'' are a sheafified form of [[sheaf cohomology]] in this case with proper (compact) support; they are bundled up into a single functor by means of the [[derived category]] formulation of [[homological algebra]] (introduced with this case in mind). If <math>f</math> is proper, then
<math>Rf_{!} = Rf_{\ast}</math> is a right adjoint to the ''inverse image'' functor <math>f^{\ast}</math>. The ''existence theorem'' for the twisted inverse image is the name given to the proof of the existence for what would be the [[counit]] for the [[comonad]] of the sought-for adjunction, namely a [[natural transformation]]

:<math>Rf_{!}f^{!}\rightarrow id</math>,

which is denoted by <math>Tr_f</math> (Hartshorne) or <math>\int_f</math> (Verdier). It is the aspect of the theory closest to the classical meaning, as the notation suggests, that duality is defined by integration.

To be more precise, <math>f^{!}</math> exists as an [[exact functor]] from a derived category of [[quasi-coherent sheaves]] on <math>Y</math>, to the analogous category on <math>X</math>, whenever

:<math>f : X \rightarrow Y</math>

is a proper or quasi-projective morphism of [[noetherian scheme]]s, of finite [[Krull dimension]].<ref>{{Harvard citations|last = Verdier|year = 1969|nb = yes}}, an elegant and more general approach was found by Amnon Neeman, by using methods from algebraic topology notably [[Brown representability]], see {{Harvard citations|last=Neeman|year=1996|nb=yes}}</ref> From this the rest of the theory can be derived: dualizing complexes pull back via <math>f^{!}</math>, the [[Grothendieck residue symbol]], the dualizing sheaf in the [[Cohen–Macaulay]] case.

In order to get a statement in more classical language, but still wider than Serre duality, Hartshorne (''Algebraic Geometry'') uses the [[Ext_functor#Important_special_cases|Ext functor of sheaves]]; this is a kind of stepping stone to the derived category.

The classical statement of Grothendieck duality for a projective or proper morphism <math>f : X \rightarrow Y</math> of noetherian schemes of finite dimension, found in Hartshorne (''Residues and duality'') is the following quasi-isomorphism

:<math>Rf_{\ast}RHom_X(F^\bullet,f^! G^\bullet)\to RHom_Y(Rf_{\ast}F^\bullet ,G^\bullet)</math>

for <math>F^\bullet</math> a bounded above complex of <math>O_X</math>-modules with quasi-coherent cohomology and <math>G^\bullet</math> a bounded below complex of <math>O_Y</math>-modules with coherent cohomology.  Here the <math>Hom</math>'s are sheaves of homomorphisms.

==Construction of the ''f''<sup>!</sup> pseudofunctor using rigid dualizing complexes==

Over the years, several approaches for constructing the <math>f^{!}</math> pseudofunctor emerged. One quite recent successful approach is based on the notion of a rigid dualizing complex. This notion was first defined by Van den Bergh in a noncommutative context.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=van den Bergh|first1=Michel|author-link=Michel Van den Bergh|title=Existence Theorems for Dualizing Complexes over Non-commutative Graded and Filtered Rings|journal=Journal of Algebra|date=September 1997|volume=195|issue=2|pages=662–679|doi=10.1006/jabr.1997.7052|doi-access=free}}</ref> The construction is based on a variant of derived [[Hochschild cohomology]] (Shukla cohomology): Let <math>k</math> be a commutative ring, and let 
<math>A</math> be a commutative <math>k-</math>algebra. There is a functor <math>RHom_{A\otimes^L_k A}(A,M\otimes^L_k M)</math> which takes a cochain complex <math>M</math> to an object <math>RHom_{A\otimes^L_k A}(A,M\otimes^L_k M)</math> in the derived category over <math>A</math>.<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Yekutieli | first1=Amnon
| title=The Squaring Operation for Commutative DG Rings
| date=2016
| arxiv=1412.4229
| journal=Journal of Algebra
| volume=449
| pages=50–107
| doi=10.1016/j.jalgebra.2015.09.038 | doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Avramov|first1=Luchezar L.|last2=Iyengar|first2=Srikanth B.|last3=Lipman|first3=Joseph|last4=Nayak|first4=Suresh|title=Reduction of derived Hochschild functors over commutative algebras and schemes|journal=[[Advances in Mathematics]]|date=January 2010|volume=223|issue=2|pages=735–772|doi=10.1016/j.aim.2009.09.002|doi-access=free|arxiv=0904.4004|s2cid=15218584}}</ref>

Assuming <math>A</math> is noetherian, a rigid dualizing complex over <math>A</math> relative to <math>k</math> is by definition a pair <math>(R,\rho)</math> where <math>R</math> is a dualizing complex over <math>A</math> which has finite flat dimension over <math>k</math>, and where
<math>\rho: R\to RHom_{A\otimes^L_k A}(A,R\otimes^L_k R)</math> is an isomorphism in the derived category <math>D(A)</math>. If such a rigid dualizing complex exists, then it is unique in a strong sense.<ref name=Yekutieli>{{cite journal|last1=Yekutieli|first1=Amnon|last2=Zhang|first2=James J.|title=Rigid Dualizing Complexes Over Commutative Rings|journal=Algebras and Representation Theory|date=31 May 2008|volume=12|issue=1|pages=19–52|doi=10.1007/s10468-008-9102-9|arxiv=math/0601654|s2cid=13597155}}</ref>

Assuming <math>A</math> is a [[Localization of a ring|localization]] of a finite type <math>k</math>-algebra, existence of a rigid dualizing complex over <math>A</math> relative to <math>k</math> was first proved by [[Amnon Yekutieli|Yekutieli]] and Zhang<ref name=Yekutieli/> assuming <math>k</math> is a regular noetherian ring of finite Krull dimension, and by [[Luchezar L. Avramov|Avramov]], Iyengar and [[Joseph Lipman|Lipman]]<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Avramov|first1=Luchezar|last2=Iyengar|first2=Srikanth|last3=Lipman|first3=Joseph|title=Reflexivity and rigidity for complexes, I: Commutative rings|journal=Algebra & Number Theory|date=14 January 2010|volume=4|issue=1|pages=47–86|doi=10.2140/ant.2010.4.47|arxiv=0904.4695|s2cid=18255441}}</ref> assuming <math>k</math> is a [[Gorenstein ring]] of finite Krull dimension and <math>A</math> is of finite flat dimension over <math>k</math>.

If <math>X</math> is a scheme of finite type over <math>k</math>, one can glue the rigid dualizing complexes that its affine pieces have,<!-- <ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=Yekutieli|first1=Amnon|last2=Zhang|first2=James J.|title=Rigid dualizing complexes on schemes|date=2004|eprint=math/0405570}}</ref> --><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Avramov|first1=Luchezar|last2=Iyengar|first2=Srikanth|last3=Lipman|first3=Joseph|title=Reflexivity and rigidity for complexes, II: Schemes|journal=Algebra & Number Theory|date=10 September 2011|volume=5|issue=3|pages=379–429|doi=10.2140/ant.2011.5.379|arxiv=1001.3450|s2cid=21639634}}</ref> and obtain a rigid dualizing complex <math>R_X</math>. Once one establishes a global existence of a rigid dualizing complex, given a map <math>f:X\to Y</math> of schemes over <math>k</math>, one can define <math>f^{!} := D_X \circ Lf^* \circ D_Y</math>, where for a scheme <math>X</math>, we set <math>D_X:= RHom_{\mathcal{O}_X}(-,R_X)</math>.

== Dualizing complex examples ==

=== Dualizing complex for a projective variety ===
The dualizing complex for a projective variety <math>X \subset \mathbb{P}^n</math> is given by the complex
:<math>\omega_X^\bullet = \mathrm{RHom}_{\mathbb{P}^n}(\mathcal{O}_X,\omega_{\mathbb{P}^n}[+n])</math>
<ref>{{cite web|last1=Kovacs|first1=Sandor|title=Singularities of stable varieties|url=https://sites.math.washington.edu/~kovacs/2013/papers/Kovacs__Singularities_of_stable_varieties.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170822172544/https://sites.math.washington.edu/~kovacs/2013/papers/Kovacs__Singularities_of_stable_varieties.pdf|archive-date=2017-08-22}}</ref>

=== Plane intersecting a line ===
Consider the projective variety
:<math>X = \text{Proj}\left( \frac{\mathbb{C}[x,y,z,w]}{(x)(y,z)} \right) = \text{Proj}\left( \frac{\mathbb{C}[x,y,z,w]}{(xy,xz)} \right)</math>
We can compute <math>\mathrm{RHom}_{\mathbb{P}^3}(\mathcal{O}_X,\omega_{\mathbb{P}^3}[+3])</math> using a resolution <math>\mathcal{L}^\bullet \to \mathcal{O}_X</math> by locally free sheaves. This is given by the complex
:<math>
0 \to \mathcal{O}(-3) \xrightarrow{\begin{bmatrix}z \\ -y \end{bmatrix}} \mathcal{O}(-2) \oplus \mathcal{O}(-2) \xrightarrow{\begin{bmatrix}xy & xz \end{bmatrix}} \mathcal{O} \to \mathcal{O}_X \to 0
</math>
Since <math>\omega_{\mathbb{P}^3} \cong \mathcal{O}(-4)</math> we have that
:<math>
\omega_X^\bullet = \mathrm{RHom}_{\mathbb{P}^3}(\mathcal{L}^\bullet, \mathcal{O}(-4)[+3]) = \mathrm{RHom}_{\mathbb{P}^3}(\mathcal{L}^\bullet\otimes \mathcal{O}(4)[-3], \mathcal{O})
</math>
This is the complex
:<math>
[\mathcal{O}(-4) \xrightarrow{\begin{bmatrix}xy \\ xz \end{bmatrix}} \mathcal{O}(-2) \oplus \mathcal{O}(-2) 
\xrightarrow{\begin{bmatrix}z & -y \end{bmatrix}} \mathcal{O}(-1)][-3]</math>
